Author: Claire Fry Published: 10:05 PM EDT April 4, 2025 Updated: 10:32 PM EDT April 4, 2025 GREENSBORO, N.C. Springs Are Warming As spring continues to unfold across the United States, a clear trend has emerged: its getting warmer. This isn't just about a few unseasonably warm days here and thereit's about a consistent rise in temperatures across the country. According to Climate Central, since 1970, average spring temperatures have increased in 97% of the U.S. cities they analyzed. In that time, spring temperatures have warmed by nearly 2.5F across 234 cities. In North Carolina, the temperature shift is even more pronounced, with spring temperatures rising by 3.5F between 1970 and 2024. While a few extra warm days might sound nice, this shift has significant implications for our environment, health, and daily lives. On average, were experiencing 17 more days of above-normal temperatures than we did back in 1970, and this trend is only expected to continue. This warming pattern has several noticeable effects. - For one, warmer springs can exacerbate seasonal allergies. A longer growing season means plants have more time to release pollen, which could leave you reaching for the tissues earlier in the year. - Additionally, these conditions worsen the risk of wildfires. With high heat, low humidity, and strong winds, wildfires can start and spread fastermaking spring the fastest-growing fire season across many U.S. regions. - And here's something you might not expect: warmer springs also contribute to an increase in mosquito populations. While cold winters typically help control mosquito numbers, warmer temperatures can extend their season, leading to a rise in health risks associated with these pests. As spring temperatures continue to rise, it's crucial to understand these patterns and prepare for more frequent above-normal days. With rising temperatures, it's clear that our springs are changing in ways that can affect us all. Stay informed and preparedthis is just the beginning of a warmer future. Springs Are Warming As spring continues to unfold across the United States, a clear trend has emerged: its getting warmer. This isn't just about a few unseasonably warm days here and thereit's about a consistent rise in temperatures across the country. According to Climate Central, since 1970, average spring temperatures have increased in 97% of the U.S. cities they analyzed. In that time, spring temperatures have warmed by nearly 2.5F across 234 cities. In North Carolina, the temperature shift is even more pronounced, with spring temperatures rising by 3.5F between 1970 and 2024. While a few extra warm days might sound nice, this shift has significant implications for our environment, health, and daily lives. On average, were experiencing 17 more days of above-normal temperatures than we did back in 1970, and this trend is only expected to continue. This warming pattern has several noticeable effects. - For one, warmer springs can exacerbate seasonal allergies. A longer growing season means plants have more time to release pollen, which could leave you reaching for the tissues earlier in the year. - Additionally, these conditions worsen the risk of wildfires. With high heat, low humidity, and strong winds, wildfires can start and spread fastermaking spring the fastest-growing fire season across many U.S. regions. - And here's something you might not expect: warmer springs also contribute to an increase in mosquito populations. While cold winters typically help control mosquito numbers, warmer temperatures can extend their season, leading to a rise in health risks associated with these pests. As spring temperatures continue to rise, it's crucial to understand these patterns and prepare for more frequent above-normal days. With rising temperatures, it's clear that our springs are changing in ways that can affect us all. Stay informed and preparedthis is just the beginning of a warmer future.
